title: Landscape characteristics influence projected growth rates of stream-resident juvenile salmon in the face of climate change in the Kenai River watershed, southcentral Alaska
text:
0.1 Overview
This document is an analytical white paper supporting Meyer et al. 2023: “Landscape characteristics influence projected growth rates of stream-resident juvenile salmon in the face of climate change in the Kenai River watershed, southcentral Alaska,” published in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society. The published paper is available at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/366050916. The underlying data are archived at https://knb.ecoinformatics.org/view/doi:10.5063/F1Q52MZF.
The purpose of this document is to provide a full reproducible, narrative account of the analytical decisions, data processing steps, and exploratory findings that informed the published paper. It is not a replication of the paper itself, but is a record of exploratory data analysis.

title: Landscape characteristics influence projected growth rates of stream-resident juvenile salmon in the face of climate change in the Kenai River watershed, southcentral Alaska
text:
0.2 Study Context
Juvenile Pacific salmon rear in freshwater streams before migrating to marine environments. Their growth during this freshwater rearing period has long-term consequences for survival and productivity. In the Kenai River watershed of southcentral Alaska, projected increases in stream temperature under climate change scenarios raise concern about whether habitat there offers sufficiently resilient options to continue to support productive juvenile salmon growth.
We used a bioenergetics modeling approach to address this question: first parameterizing fish growth models with observed 2015-2016 field data (diet composition, water temperature, and fish size), then simulating growth under projected future water temperature scenarios from 2030-2039 and 2060-2069.

2.1 Overview
This chapter describes the study area, sampling design, and field methods underlying analyses in this white paper. Content is drawn from the Methods section of Meyer et al. 2023 and Chapter 1 of Meyer 2020 (University of Alaska Fairbanks M.S. thesis).
crumbs: 2  Study Area and Field Methods

title: 2  Study Area and Field Methods
text:
2.2 Overall Approach
We measured air temperature, water temperature, and the growth rates and diet composition of juvenile Chinook and Coho Salmon during May through September 2015 and 2016 at ten sites within the Kenai River watershed. Based on these field data, we simulated juvenile growth during summer under current conditions using coupled stream temperature models and bioenergetic models. We then compared the relative changes in growth from a 2010-2019 baseline period to those projected under various future temperature and feeding rate scenarios for the 2030-2039 and 2060-2069 decades.
The stream temperature model generated monthly stream temperatures which were input as daily values to a bioenergetic model that predicted the daily growth rate and size of idealized juvenile Chinook or Coho Salmon. Our model used field-based empirical inputs for food, temperature, and fish size across geographically diverse habitats within the Kenai River watershed, emphasizing the diversity of food and water temperature conditions across space and time.

The Kenai River drains an area of 5,568 km2 in southcentral Alaska, running 182 km west from the Kenai Mountains and emptying into Cook Inlet near the city of Kenai. The watershed supports commercial, sport, subsistence, and personal-use fisheries.

title: 2  Study Area and Field Methods
text:
2.4 Field Sampling

2.4.1 Stream Temperature
We acquired water temperature data (n = 14 sites) and air temperature data (n = 11 sites) from HOBO® Temp Pro v2 loggers deployed during summers 2015 and 2016, USGS stream gauge stations at Soldotna (station ID 15266300) and Cooper Landing (station ID 15258000), and National Weather Service archives for the Kenai Airport.
Water and air temperature data were collected at a minimum of three sites per tributary and two sites in the main stem along a longitudinal gradient from lower to upper reaches, following best practices and standards described in Mauger et al. (2015). Site-specific methods for channel transect representativeness, equipment calibration, and logger check procedures are described in Appendix A of Meyer et al. 2023.


2.4.2 Juvenile Salmon Capture
We sampled juvenile Chinook (n = 1,145) and Coho Salmon (n = 2,646) within the lower, middle, and upper extent of their documented habitat in each of the three focal tributaries (Reimer 2013). Sites were also sampled in the mainstem Kenai River near the mouths of Beaver Creek and the Russian River. Exploratory sampling was conducted in lentic environments above and below Ptarmigan Creek (Ptarmigan Lake and Kenai Lake, respectively), but target species were not captured and these sites were excluded.
Fish sampling efforts were constrained to a 200-m length of stream centered around each water temperature logger site (modified as needed for low catch success or terrain). Main channel and off-channel habitats were sampled at each site. Sites were visited approximately monthly (31 ± 5 days, mean ± SD) throughout May to August 2015 and May to September 2016.
We used Gee® minnow traps baited with salmon eggs to capture juvenile salmon, an effective passive capture method in Alaska (Magnus 2006; Sethi and Benolkin 2013). Eggs were enclosed in perforated containers to permit scent to escape while preventing consumption. We suspended 12 to 20 traps at water depths of 15 to 45 cm for 2 to 4 hours per set. All salmon eggs used as bait were commercially sterilized or disinfected with a ten-minute soak in a 1/100 Betadyne solution prior to use.
Captured juvenile salmon were anesthetized by submersion in a 20 to 40 mg/L eugenol (AQUI-STM) bath for 2 to 3 minutes. We measured fork length to the nearest mm and weighed to the nearest 0.1 g. Fish recovered in aerated water and were held in-stream in a mesh basket to prevent same-day recaptures. Non-target species were identified, recorded, and released.


2.4.3 Diet Sampling (Gastric Lavage)
For a subset of juvenile Chinook (n = 219) and Coho Salmon (n = 553) we sampled scales and stomach contents to determine age and diet composition for bioenergetics models. At each monthly site visit we aimed to sample up to 16 individuals per species with fork lengths ≥ 50 mm, subject to abundance constraints.
Gut contents were flushed out of the mouth using the gastric lavage technique with a modified syringe (Culp et al. 1988) into a 250 μm sieve and preserved in a minimum of 70% ethanol in a Whirl-Pak bag.


2.4.4 Diet Sample Processing
Stomach content samples were examined under 4.0x dissecting microscopes. Distinguishable invertebrates (n = 8,879) were identified to family level or the lowest taxon feasible (112 taxon/lifestage combinations identified), and body lengths were measured to the nearest 1.0 mm (Merritt and Cummins 1996). Lengths of partially digested prey were estimated based on intact individuals of the same taxon that appeared similar in size (Wipfli 1997). When intact individuals of the same taxon were absent in a sample, head and thorax length was assumed to represent 1/3 of total length of partially digested prey (Gonzales 2006). Diet items that could not be positively attributed (e.g., exoskeletons, separated wings or legs, empty Trichoptera casings, unidentified head capsules) were recorded but excluded from diet proportions.


2.4.5 Prey Dry Mass Estimation
Diet composition was characterized in terms of mass, the most applicable metric for energy flow and food web studies (Chipps and Garvey 2007). Dry mass of individual invertebrates was estimated using the allometric formula:
\[W = aL^{b}\]
where \(W\) is total dry body mass, \(L\) is total body length, and \(a\) and \(b\) are taxon-specific constants derived from a database of over 100 genera compiled from existing literature and Alaskan stream invertebrates (Meyer 2019). For juvenile fish prey items, regression constants from the length-weight relationship developed from age-0 Coho Salmon captured in this study were used (B.E. Meyer, unpublished data).
These dry mass calculations were performed within the field data workbooks (Excel). The column Total_Prey_Dry_Mass_mg in the raw data sheets is the output of these formula-based calculations.


2.4.6 Prey Wet Mass and Diet Categories
Prey item dry mass was converted to wet mass using the wet/dry mass ratios published by McCarthy et al. (2009) and additional literature sources. This conversion is documented in full in Chapter 3 (Diet Composition).
Diet composition was summarized using five categories for bioenergetics modeling:

2.4.7 Juvenile Salmon Age and Growth
We aged scales from the subset of fish selected for stomach content analysis and used length-age relationships to assign individual fish an age (Quist et al. 2012). Age thresholds for distinguishing age-0 from age-1 fish were determined visually from length-frequency distributions. Methods for scale ageing and age cohort prediction for unaged fish are described in Appendix C of Meyer et al. 2023.
Age-2 Coho Salmon and age-1 Chinook Salmon were excluded from bioenergetics analyses, as these cohorts were anticipated to be almost exclusively pre-smolt outmigrants with small sample sizes (Shields and Dupuis 2017).

title: 3  Diet Composition: Literature Review
text:
3.1 Overview
Juvenile Pacific salmon rearing in freshwater streams consume a mix of prey originating from aquatic, terrestrial, and in some rivers, marine sources. The relative contributions of these subsidies vary with season, river type, riparian vegetation, and fish species and size. Understanding how these proportions vary across space and time is central to interpreting the bioenergetics inputs used in Meyer et al. 2023, and to characterizing the prey base available to juvenile Chinook and Coho salmon in the Kenai River watershed.
This chapter reviews published literature on juvenile salmon diet composition, with a focus on:
Findings from this review inform the scope and presentation of the 2015-2016 diet composition summaries developed in subsequent chapters.

title: 3  Diet Composition: Literature Review
text:
How prey subsidies from terrestrial, freshwater-aquatic, and marine sources are partitioned
How those partitions vary across seasons, rivers, habitats, and fish attributes
How authors have presented these data (metrics, visualization approaches)

title: 3  Diet Composition: Literature Review
text:
3.2 Key Papers

3.2.1 Rine et al. 2016: Susitna River, Alaska
Full citation: Rine, K.M., Wipfli, M.S., Schoen, E.R., Nightengale, T.L., and Stricker, C.A. 2016. Trophic pathways supporting juvenile Chinook and coho salmon in the glacial Susitna River, Alaska: patterns of freshwater, marine, and terrestrial food resource use across a seasonally dynamic habitat mosaic. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences 73(11): 1626–1641. https://doi.org/10.1139/cjfas-2015-0555
Author’s note: B. Meyer was a field technician for this study.
Relevance: High. Examines the same two species (Chinook, Coho) in a large south-central Alaska river system (Susitna), across multiple seasons and macrohabitat types. Integrates stable isotope analysis with stomach content data.
Methods summary:

Spatial coverage: 97 km segment of the Susitna River; multiple macrohabitat types (tributary mouths, side sloughs, upland sloughs, side channels, main channel)
Temporal coverage: multiple sampling events across the rearing season
Analytical methods: stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) combined with gut content analysis
Prey classification: freshwater-derived, marine-derived, and terrestrial-derived

Key findings:

Juvenile salmon were supported primarily by freshwater-derived resources and secondarily by marine and terrestrial sources (Rine et al. 2016).
The relative contribution of marine-derived prey was greatest in the fall within off-channel macrohabitats, whereas contributions of terrestrial invertebrate prey were generally greatest during midsummer, across all macrohabitats (Rine et al. 2016).

Presentation approach:

Prey subsidies presented as proportional contributions to diet by source (freshwater, marine, terrestrial)
Results disaggregated by macrohabitat type, season, and fish species
Both isotope mixing model outputs and stomach content proportions reported

Notes for our analysis: Our Kenai 2015-2016 data does not include stable isotope data, so we rely entirely on stomach content proportions. We lack the spatial complexity of multiple macrohabitat types within rivers, but we have multiple rivers and reaches within the Kenai watershed and multiple seasons. The three-way categorization (freshwater-aquatic, marine, terrestrial) used by Rine et al. maps reasonably well onto our prey categories.



3.2.2 Grunblatt et al. 2019: Kenai River Watershed, Alaska
Full citation: Grunblatt, J., B.E. Meyer, and M.S. Wipfli. 2019. Invertebrate prey contributions to juvenile Coho Salmon diet from riparian habitats along three Alaska streams: implications for environmental change. Journal of Freshwater Ecology 34(1):617-631. https://doi.org/10.1080/02705060.2019.1642243
Author’s note: B. Meyer is a co-author on this paper. Its data are the same as what is presented in Meyer et al. 2023.
Relevance: Very high. This study was conducted within the Kenai River watershed of southcentral Alaska and determined the proportion of total diet for stream-rearing juvenile Coho Salmon derived from terrestrial and aquatic winged adult invertebrates across three streams representative of habitats found throughout the region (Grunblatt et al. 2019).
Methods summary:

Species: Coho Salmon only
Sampling: seasonal stomach content sampling across two years
Prey classification: terrestrial invertebrates, aquatic winged adults, benthic aquatic invertebrates
Riparian habitat classification: grass/sedge, shrub, tree

Key findings:

The proportion of juvenile salmon diet represented by aquatic invertebrates was significantly different among study reaches, representing 62%, 55%, and 37% for Beaver Creek, Ptarmigan Creek, and the Russian River, respectively
Aquatic winged adult prey contributions were significantly lower in the grass/sedge study reach, and cross-ecosystem invertebrate prey represented a significantly higher proportion of diet in the tree study reach

Presentation approach:

Diet proportions presented by prey origin category (terrestrial, aquatic winged adult, benthic aquatic) across reaches and seasons
Statistical comparisons (ANOVA) among reaches for each prey category
Results disaggregated by study reach (river), not by fish species, age, or size class





3.2.3 Clitherow et al. 2024: Glacier Bay, Alaska
Full citation: Clitherow, L.R., S.H. Sønderland, F.M. Windsor, and A.M. Milner. 2024. Variation in the diet of juvenile salmonids across a gradient of stream development in Glacier Bay, Alaska. Pages 85-112 in A.J. Dumbrell and A.M. Milner, editors. Stream research in Glacier Bay, Alaska from 1977-2024: part 2. Advances in Ecological Research 71. https://doi.org/10.1016/bs.aecr.2024.10.005
Relevance: Moderate. Examines Coho salmon and Dolly Varden diets across streams of varying age since deglaciation, using gut content analysis combined with stable isotopes.
Key findings:

Juvenile salmonids, particularly coho salmon, in streams with higher channel sinuosity consumed a higher proportion of terrestrial prey
Patterns in diet reflected geomorphology, vegetational properties, and periodic disturbances in the watersheds

Presentation approach: Combines gut content analysis and stable isotope data to characterize dietary niche and prey source contributions across a stream development gradient.
Notes for our analysis: Reinforces the expectation that landscape-level factors (channel form, riparian vegetation) mediate terrestrial prey inputs, directly relevant to the landscape ecology framing of Meyer et al. 2023.



3.2.4 Duffy et al. 2010: Puget Sound Chinook Salmon
Full citation: Duffy, E.J., D.A. Beauchamp, R.M. Sweeting, R.J. Beamish, and J.S. Brennan. 2010. Ontogenetic diet shifts of juvenile Chinook salmon in nearshore and offshore habitats of Puget Sound. Transactions of the American Fisheries Society 139(3): 803-823. https://doi.org/10.1577/T08-244.1
Relevance: Moderate. Marine setting rather than freshwater, but provides a well-documented example of how diet composition data for Chinook salmon are analyzed and visualized across spatial and temporal groupings.
Key findings:

ANOVA was used to examine the effects of year, month, region, habitat, and size-class on proportions of prey groups in the diet of juvenile Chinook salmon.
Monthly diet composition was presented as wet-weight proportions of each prey category, disaggregated by region, with sample size and average fish length annotated on each bar.

Presentation approach: Stacked bar charts of wet-weight proportions, faceted by region (north, central, south), with time (month) on the x-axis. This is a clear example of the standard multi-panel format for presenting diet proportions across multiple grouping variables.
Notes for our analysis: Wet-weight proportions are the appropriate metric given our dry-to-wet mass conversion. The multi-panel stacked bar approach (faceted by a spatial or biological variable, with season on the x-axis) is a reasonable visualization format.



3.2.5 Kennedy et al. 2018: Eelgrass Habitat, Pacific Salmon
Full citation: Kennedy, L.A., F. Juanes, and R. El-Sabaawi. 2018. Eelgrass as valuable nearshore foraging habitat for juvenile Pacific salmon in the early marine period. Marine and Coastal Fisheries 10(2): 190-203. https://doi.org/10.1002/mcf2.10018
Relevance: Low-moderate. Marine context, but documents a common visualization approach.
Presentation approach: The proportion of each invertebrate group by count was assessed in juvenile salmon diets using a stacked bar graph. The proportion of total abundance of eelgrass-associated, planktonic, and terrestrial invertebrates in juvenile Chum and Chinook Salmon diets were calculated and presented alongside stable isotope mixing model results.
Notes for our analysis: Proportions by count (numerical) are an alternative to proportions by mass. Our raw data include both prey quantity (count) and prey dry mass. On energetic grounds, and for consistency with bioenergetics model inputs, mass-based proportions are the appropriate primary metric.



3.2.6 Syrjänen et al. 2011: Terrestrial Prey in Salmonid Diets
Full citation: Syrjänen, J., K. Korsu, P. Louhi, R. Paavola, and T. Muotka. 2011. Stream salmonids as opportunistic foragers: the importance of terrestrial invertebrates along a stream-size gradient. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences 68(12): 2146-2156. https://doi.org/10.1139/f2011-118
Key finding: In a quantitative literature review, the mean proportion of terrestrial prey in salmonid diets was 17%, being highest for the largest fish (≥15 cm).
Notes for our analysis: This provides a useful cross-study baseline. We have fish length data, so we can explore whether terrestrial prey proportion increases with fish size in our dataset.

title: 3  Diet Composition: Literature Review
text:
3.3 Summary: Methods and Presentation Conventions

3.3.1 Metric for proportions
The most common metric is wet mass (or wet weight). Proportions by count are also used but are considered less informative for energetic modeling given the large size variation among prey items. Our dry-to-wet mass conversion produces the appropriate metric.


3.3.2 Prey categorization
Studies vary in granularity:

Coarse (3 groups): terrestrial, freshwater-aquatic, marine (used by Rine et al. 2016)
Intermediate (4–6 groups): e.g., separating aquatic larvae from aquatic adults, or distinguishing fish/eggs from invertebrates (common in gut-content-focused studies)
Fine (taxon-level): used in ordination or multivariate analyses, not typically in proportion summaries

Our prey categories (diet1: FishEggs, diet2: InvertAquatic_AqOrigin, diet3: InvertTerrestrial, diet4: InvertTerrestrial_AqOrigin, diet5: SalmonEggs) align with an intermediate scheme. We will present results at both the coarse level (terrestrial vs. aquatic vs. marine subsidy) and the intermediate level.


3.3.3 Analytical approaches
Most freshwater studies rely on gut content proportions alone. Stable isotope analysis corroborates or extends gut content findings but requires substantially more resources. Our study used gut content only, which is appropriate and typical for bioenergetics modeling contexts.

title: 3  Diet Composition: Literature Review
text:
3.4 Implications for 2015-2016 Diet Composition Analysis
Based on this review, the analysis chapters that follow will:

Present diet proportions as wet-mass-based proportions (proportion of total wet mass from each prey category per fish or group of fish)
Adopt a two-level prey grouping: coarse (terrestrial / freshwater-aquatic / marine) and intermediate (the five bioenergetics diet categories)
Disaggregate results by season × river × species × age where sample sizes allow
Present primary visualizations as stacked bar charts, faceted by species and/or age, with season on the x-axis
Compare observed proportions against the cross-study baseline (~17% terrestrial, with higher values for larger fish and in late summer)


Full citations for all works referenced in this chapter are collated in the References chapter.

4.2 Data Import
We import diet contents data from the two primary field data workbooks. Columns are selected and renamed to a consistent lowercase schema. Both years are combined into a single data frame before any transformations.
The two source files are:

other/inputs/diet_size_other/2015 EPSCoR SCTC.xlsx (sheet: “2015 Diet Contents Data”)
other/inputs/diet_size_other/2016_EPSCoR_Aquatic_Ecology_Database.xlsx (sheet: “2016 Diet Contents Data”)

Dry mass values in these sheets were estimated from measured prey item lengths using length-weight regressions (W = aL^b), where parameters were drawn from the literature. These calculations were performed within the Excel workbooks using formula-based pipelines. The resulting Total_Prey_Dry_Mass_mg column is our starting point.


Code
SCTC2015 <- "other/inputs/diet_size_other/2015 EPSCoR SCTC.xlsx"
SCTC2016 <- "other/inputs/diet_size_other/2016_EPSCoR_Aquatic_Ecology_Database.xlsx"

diet15 <- read_excel(SCTC2015, sheet = "2015 Diet Contents Data") |>
  select(
    Sample.ID, Fish_Species, Sample.Event, sample.event.num,
    River, Reach, Site, Sample_Date, Prey_Type_Used, PreyCategory,
    Quantity, Total_Prey_Dry_Mass_mg
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = "2015",
    sample.event.num = as.integer(sample.event.num),
    Quantity = as.numeric(Quantity),
    Total_Prey_Dry_Mass_mg = as.numeric(Total_Prey_Dry_Mass_mg)

  select(
    Sample.ID, Fish_Species, Sample.Event, sample.event.num,
    River, Reach, Site, Sample_Date, Prey_Type_Used, PreyCategory,
    Quantity, Total_Prey_Dry_Mass_mg
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = "2016",
    sample.event.num = as.integer(sample.event.num)
  )

diet <- bind_rows(diet15, diet16) |>
  rename(
    sample.id  = Sample.ID,
    spp        = Fish_Species,
    sample.event = Sample.Event,
    event.num  = sample.event.num,

4.7 Summary Figures

4.7.1 Prey Composition by River, Season, and Age
The primary visualization is a stacked bar chart of mean wet-mass proportions, faceted by river (column) and age class (row), with season on the x-axis. We present this three ways: Coho only, Chinook only, and with both species’ diet content pooled together, since cross-species comparison is not the focus of this deliverable and faceting by species as well made facet strip labels illegible. Age classes remain separate in all three. See the literature review chapter for context on this presentation format.

  SalmonEggs                 = "Salmon Eggs",
  FishEggs                   = "Fish Eggs",
  InvertAquatic_AqOrigin     = "Immature Aquatic",
  InvertTerrestrial_AqOrigin = "Adult Aquatic",
  InvertTerrestrial          = "Terrestrial"
)

preycat_colors <- c(
  SalmonEggs                 = "#b2182b",
  FishEggs                   = "#ef8a62",
  InvertAquatic_AqOrigin     = "#4393c3",
  InvertTerrestrial_AqOrigin = "#92c5de",
  InvertTerrestrial          = "#1a9850"
)

# Shared summary + plotting helpers for the three diet composition figures below
summarise_diet <- function(data) {
  data |>
    group_by(river, season, age, preycat) |>
    summarise(
      mean_prop = mean(prop_wm, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_fish    = n_distinct(sample.id),
      .groups   = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      season = factor(season, levels = c(
        "Early Summer", "Mid-Summer", "Late Summer", "Fall")),
      age_label = paste0("Age ", age)
    )
}

plot_diet_bars <- function(data) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = season, y = mean_prop, fill = preycat)) +
    geom_col(position = "stack") +
    geom_text(
      aes(label = n_fish, group = preycat),
      stat = "summary", fun = sum,
      position = position_stack(vjust = 1.05),
      size = 2.5, check_overlap = TRUE
    ) +
    facet_grid(age_label ~ river) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = preycat_colors, labels = preycat_labels) +
    labs(
      x = "Season",
      y = "Mean proportion of diet (wet mass)",
      fill = "Prey category"
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))
}

text:
4.10 Notes and Data Quality

Prey items that could not be assigned a wet/dry ratio (i.e., did not match any entry in the conversion table) are excluded from all wet-mass calculations. This includes placeholder/non-prey entries recorded as Bait, Bait EGGS, Empty/EMPTY, and 0 (empty-stomach or bait-contamination codes), which have no conversion-table match and are dropped naturally at that step.
The preycat field used throughout this chapter is the bioenergetics diet-slot classification (PreyCategory_ED) from the conversion workbook, not the raw field-recorded PreyCategory column (kept as preycat_field); the two classification schemes disagree for some taxa (e.g., oligochaetes), and only PreyCategory_ED is used for FB4 diet-slot inputs.
Fish without an assigned age (Age_manual2 = NA) are excluded from age-disaggregated summaries.
Per-fish diet proportions are completed with explicit zeros for uneaten prey categories before group-level averaging (see the Diet Proportions section); without this step, stacked group means do not sum to 100%.
Age-2 Coho and age-1 Chinook are excluded from the analysis following Meyer et al. 2023 (these cohorts are sparse and likely transitioning out of freshwater rearing).

5.5 Generating FB4 Input Files
The code below generates the per-simulation Temperature.csv and Diet_prop.csv files, as well as the static Pred_E.csv, Prey_E.csv, and Indigestible_Prey.csv files. This code creates and populates the other/FB4_1.1.3_2015_2016.1/ directory.
These files are already committed to the repository. Run this section only if regenerating inputs from scratch.

5.5.1 Daily diet and temperature by simulation day


Code
# Read diet and temporal extent data
obs_diet_props <- read.csv("other/outputs/observed_diet_proportions.csv") |>
  mutate(days = as.double(days))

# Expand diet proportions to one row per simulation day
sim_diet_days <- obs_diet_props[
  rep(seq_len(nrow(obs_diet_props)), obs_diet_props[, "days"]), ] |>
  mutate(
    sim_name = paste0(year, "_", season, "_", site, "_", spp, "_Age_", age)
  ) |>
  group_by(sim_name) |>
  mutate(
    SimDay = row_number(),
    Date   = as.Date(sim.start) + lubridate::days(SimDay)
  ) |>
  mutate(year_chr = as.character(year(Date)))

# Join daily water temperatures
sim_diet_days <- left_join(
  sim_diet_days,
  daily_mean_temps |> mutate(year_chr = as.character(year)),
  by = c("Date", "site", "Stream_Name", "year_chr")
) |>
  rename(
    diet1 = FishEggs,
    diet2 = InvertAquatic_AqOrigin,
    diet3 = InvertTerrestrial,
    diet4 = InvertTerrestrial_AqOrigin,
    diet5 = SalmonEggs,
    Temp  = daily_avg_temp
  ) |>
  mutate(diet6 = 0, diet7 = 0, diet8 = 0, diet9 = 0, diet10 = 0) |>
  filter(!is.na(Temp)) |>
  select(SimDay, Temp, diet1, diet2, diet3, diet4, diet5,
         diet6, diet7, diet8, diet9, diet10, sim_name, spp)

sim_diet_days[is.na(sim_diet_days)] <- 0

# Subset to simulations in sim_size_inputs_v2
sim_size_list <- read_excel(
  "other/inputs/diet_size_other/sim_size_inputs_v2.xlsx",
  sheet = "lw_data"
) |> select(sim)

sim_diet_days <- sim_diet_days |>
  rename(sim = sim_name) |>
  inner_join(sim_size_list, by = "sim") |>
  rename(sim_name = sim) |>
  distinct()




5.5.2 Export per-simulation Temperature.csv and Diet_prop.csv


Code
sim_dir  <- "other/FB4_1.1.3_2015_2016.1/"
chnk_dir <- paste0(sim_dir, "chnk/")
coho_dir <- paste0(sim_dir, "coho/")

# Create directory structure
unlink(chnk_dir, recursive = TRUE)
unlink(coho_dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(chnk_dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(coho_dir, recursive = TRUE)

export_sim_files <- function(sim_days, spp_filter, spp_dir, file_prefix) {
  df <- sim_days |>
    filter(spp == spp_filter) |>
    select(-spp)

  # Temperature files
  temps <- df |>
    select(SimDay, Temp, sim_name) |>
    rename(day = SimDay, temperature = Temp) |>
    group_by(sim_name)

  temps_list <- split(select(temps, -sim_name),
                      temps$sim_name)

  # Diet proportion files
  diets <- df |>
    select(-Temp) |>
    rename(day = SimDay) |>
    group_by(sim_name)

  diets_list <- split(select(diets, -sim_name),
                      diets$sim_name)

  sim_names <- names(temps_list)

  # Create subdirectory for each simulation
  sim_dirs <- file.path(spp_dir, sim_names)
  Map(dir.create, sim_dirs, showWarnings = FALSE)

  # Write files
  mapply(
    function(dat, nm) {
      d <- file.path(spp_dir, nm)
      write.csv(temps_list[[nm]], file.path(d, "Temperature.csv"),
                row.names = FALSE)
      write.csv(diets_list[[nm]], file.path(d, "Diet_prop.csv"),
                row.names = FALSE)
    },
    sim_dirs, sim_names
  )
}

export_sim_files(sim_diet_days, "Chinook", chnk_dir, "chnk")
export_sim_files(sim_diet_days, "Coho",    coho_dir, "coho")

NoteManual step: Running FB4 v1.1.3



After generating the input files above, simulations are executed using the FB4 v1.1.3 graphical interface:

Download FB4 v1.1.3 from fishbioenergetics.org

Load the design file design_2015_2016_final.csv using the multi-simulation interface

New parameters: Plumb & Moffitt (2015) → FB4_2015_2016_models_new_parameters.csv

Both output files are committed to the repository and read in Chapter 6 (Simulation Results).

6.1 Overview
This chapter generates FB4 input files for projected future climate scenarios. The approach mirrors Chapter 4 (observed inputs) with two key differences:
Three temperature scenarios × three consumption scenarios = nine model runs per cohort.
Temperature scenarios:
Each period is simulated under RCP 6.0 and RCP 8.5, giving six temperature × decade combinations.
All input files are committed to other/FB4_1.1.3_projected.1/. Code that writes to disk is marked eval: false.

text:

6.2 Projected Temperature Inputs

  select(scenario, decade, month, Site, proj_h2o_Temp_C) |>

    h2o_se = plotrix::std.error(proj_h2o_Temp_C, na.rm = TRUE),

export_proj_files <- function(sim_days, spp_filter, spp_dir) {
  df <- sim_days |> filter(spp == spp_filter) |> select(-spp)
  sim_names <- unique(df$sim_name)
  sim_subdirs <- file.path(spp_dir, sim_names)
  Map(dir.create, sim_subdirs, showWarnings = FALSE)

  for (nm in sim_names) {
    d <- file.path(spp_dir, nm)
    sub_df <- df |> filter(sim_name == nm) |> select(-sim_name)
    write.csv(sub_df |> select(SimDay, Temp) |> rename(day = SimDay, temperature = Temp),
              file.path(d, "Temperature.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
    write.csv(sub_df |> rename(day = SimDay),
              file.path(d, "Diet_prop.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  }
}

7.6 Table S5: Percent Change in Final Mass by Scenario
Change in simulated final mass relative to the 2010-2019 baseline, for each projected scenario (Stewart & Ibarra parameters).


Code
pct_chg_tbl <- dat |>
  filter(scenario != "observed", parameters == "stewart_ibarra") |>
  mutate(population = paste("Age", age, spp)) |>
  select(stream_name, reach, population, year, scenario,
         consumption_scenario, final_weight_g) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = "year", values_from = "final_weight_g") |>
  unchop(everything()) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c("2030_2039", "2060_2069"),
    names_to  = "year",
    values_to = "final_mass_g"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pct_chg_mass = ((final_mass_g - `2010_2019`) / `2010_2019`),
    year = case_when(
      year == "2030_2039" ~ "2030-2039",
      year == "2060_2069" ~ "2060-2069"
    ),
    consumption_scenario = case_when(
      consumption_scenario == "mean"     ~ "Mean",
      consumption_scenario == "20minus"  ~ "-20%",
      consumption_scenario == "20plus"   ~ "+20%"
    ),
    scenario = case_when(
      scenario == "rcp60" ~ "RCP 6.0",
      scenario == "rcp85" ~ "RCP 8.5"
    )
  ) |>
  rename(
    Watershed                  = stream_name,
    Reach                      = reach,
    Population                 = population,
    `Simulation Period`        = year,
    `Climate Scenario`         = scenario,
    `Food Consumption Scenario` = consumption_scenario,
    `Percent Change in Mass`   = pct_chg_mass
  ) |>
  select(-`2010_2019`, -final_mass_g) |>
  relocate(Watershed, Reach, Population,
           `Simulation Period`, `Climate Scenario`,
           `Food Consumption Scenario`, `Percent Change in Mass`) |>
  arrange(Watershed, Reach, Population,
          `Simulation Period`, `Climate Scenario`, `Food Consumption Scenario`)

pct_chg <- read.csv("other/outputs/pct_chg_tbl.csv") |>
  clean_names() |>
  filter(climate_scenario == "RCP 8.5") |>
  mutate(
    percent_change_in_mass = as.numeric(
      str_remove(percent_change_in_mass, "%")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(watershed, population, simulation_period, food_consumption_scenario) |>
  summarise(
    mean_pct = mean(percent_change_in_mass),
    se_pct   = plotrix::std.error(percent_change_in_mass),
    .groups  = "drop"

pct_chg$food_consumption_scenario <- factor(
  pct_chg$food_consumption_scenario,
  levels = c("-20%", "Mean", "+20%")
)

ggplot(pct_chg, aes(watershed, mean_pct, fill = food_consumption_scenario)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge()) +
  geom_errorbar(

    position = position_dodge(0.9)
